items.title: Gli Stati Uniti hanno ritirato tutti i propri bombardieri dalla base inglese di Fairford
items.summary: Lo hanno deciso dopo gli arresti per un presunto piano per attaccare la struttura, usata tra le altre cose anche per la guerra in Iran
items.content:
Domenica il dipartimento della Difesa statunitense ha detto di aver ritirato tutti i bombardieri dalla base aeronautica di Fairford, nell’Inghilterra sudoccidentale. La base, oltre che dalla Royal Air Force (RAF) britannica, è usata dall’aviazione statunitense, di recente anche per i bombardieri impiegati negli attacchi contro l’Iran.

Ufficialmente non sono state date spiegazioni sul ritiro, che è stato però deciso una settimana dopo gli arresti legati a un presunto piano per attaccare la struttura. Secondo un funzionario statunitense citato da CNN , il ritiro sarebbe stato deciso dopo una nuova minaccia, di cui non sono stati resi noti i dettagli.

Nella notte tra il 26 e il 27 settembre, nei pressi della base, erano stati arrestati cinque cittadini britannici tra i 23 e i 25 anni, liberati su cauzione il giorno seguente. La polizia non ha ancora chiarito cosa stessero facendo né quale fosse il loro eventuale piano. Sabato era stato rilasciato su cauzione un altro uomo, di 25 anni e con doppia cittadinanza britannica e iraniana, arrestato due giorni prima perché sospettato di essere coinvolto nel piano. Le indagini su tutti e sei sono ancora in corso.

La base di Fairford è da tempo oggetto di proteste perché viene utilizzata dai bombardieri statunitensi impegnati nella guerra contro l’Iran. Il primo ministro britannico Andy Burnham aveva detto che erano emersi indizi di un possibile coinvolgimento iraniano nel presunto piano. Il governo iraniano ha negato le accuse, definendole infondate, e convocato l’ambasciatore britannico a Teheran per protestare

Fairford è una base utilizzata dall’aeronautica statunitense per le operazioni a lungo raggio. Il governo britannico ne aveva autorizzato l’impiego per attaccare le postazioni missilistiche iraniane da cui venivano colpite le navi nello stretto di Hormuz. Il dipartimento della Difesa statunitense ha precisato che i bombardieri rimangono in grado di compiere missioni anche partendo direttamente dagli Stati Uniti: il ritiro dalla base inglese non implica quindi, di per sé, la fine del loro impiego nella guerra.

items.title: All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
items.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.
items.content:
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.

On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.

"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."

The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.

On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.

The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).

Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.

"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."

Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.

Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.

FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.

"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"

"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.

The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.

An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".

The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".

Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.

"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

items.title: Ducati up for sale: Italy wants to bring an icon — and an emotion — back home
items.summary: Volkswagen has confirmed that it could sell the celebrated motorcycle brand as it seeks to shore up its troubled finances. Rome wants to bring the company back into Italian hands — just as it celebrates its 100th anniversary
items.content:
BOLOGNA – It is hard to put a price on an emotion. But that is precisely what Volkswagen is trying to do with Ducati, the celebrated “Red of a Thousand Victories”, cherished by an army of enthusiasts around the world. The motorcycle maker could become one of the levers — certainly not the only one, nor even the decisive one — that the German automotive group will use to pull itself out of the financial and commercial crisis it has landed in.

The Wolfsburg-based carmaker has confirmed that the Italian brand is among the assets under its control that it is considering selling to raise cash. “But nothing has been decided yet,” Volkswagen-Audi executives recently told Italian and Bologna-based authorities, which have mobilised to defend an undisputed symbol of Made in Italy.

The Italian government has said that, if Ducati is sold, it would like to bring the company “back into Italian hands”. Confindustria, Italy’s main business association, is working behind the scenes to find an Italian investment fund prepared to step in.

The aim is to try to shield from speculation a company that is, in fact, performing extremely well, has enjoyed a remarkable run of success on the track and is celebrating the centenary of its founding this year — a century-long history in which Ducati has fallen and risen again more than once.

One chapter of that story began with the arrival of Fabio Taglioni, a young engineer from Romagna who had previously worked at Mondial. Ducati’s general manager, Giuseppe Montano, did not mince his words: “I know your talent and I need you. If you can build me a 100cc motorcycle capable of winning the Giro d’Italia, we won’t have to shut down.”

There was enough money in the company’s coffers to pay just one salary.

It was 1954, and Ducati was a very long way from the global company it is today. But its passion for racing red — and for machines built with heart — was already there. And Borgo Panigale was already becoming the setting for many of the stories that would follow.

Taglioni was born in Lugo in 1920 and graduated from Bologna with a thesis on a four-cylinder racing engine. While teaching in Imola, he had even built a 75cc engine with his students. He accepted the challenge.

He designed the 100 Gran Sport — soon nicknamed the Marianna — which caused a sensation in the 125cc category at the 1955 Motogiro. A year later, in 1956, came his desmodromic valve system, destined to become one of the brand’s technical signatures.

Taglioni would remain closely associated with Ducati for decades, but he is only one of the countless figures who shaped its history. Engineers, riders, entrepreneurs and designers have often mattered as much as the motorcycles themselves.

It is difficult to say what the Red of Borgo Panigale really is today. A company, a symbol, a ritual.

When Ducati was founded in 1926, it did not make motorcycles at all. Antonio Cavalieri Ducati and his sons Adriano, Bruno and Marcello founded the Società Scientifica Radio Brevetti Ducati, specialising in communications. It was the only Italian company of its kind producing radio technology. Its small Bologna factory also manufactured a capacitor called the Manens, which became a success across five continents. Within just ten years, the small factory had grown to employ 100 workers.

In 1935, Ducati also began moving into mechanical engineering, starting with aluminium alloys. Its history is long and varied. Adriano was the technical talent of the family and experimented with shortwave radio. The company expanded rapidly: around that time it moved to its new factory in Borgo Panigale and, during the war, grew to more than 5,000 employees, becoming one of Bologna’s largest industrial companies.

Then came the bombs. The air raids of October 12, 1944, severely damaged the factory.

After the war, however, Italy needed cheap means of transport to get people moving and working again. The answer was the Cucciolo, a small four-stroke engine designed by Aldo Farinelli and later manufactured by Ducati. Fitted to a bicycle, it offered a simple, inexpensive form of mobility.

From 1946 onwards, that little engine changed the company’s destiny and set Ducati on the road to two wheels.

Time does not move in a straight line. But looking back today, Ducati has been many things. In 1948, the company also came under state control.

And here is another part of its history made up of people: from frame designer Gian Luigi Capellino to the men who transformed a radio company — which also made the Reselet electric razor, the Duofono intercom, the Duconta calculator, cameras, jukeboxes and refrigerators — into a motorcycle manufacturer.

If Ducati now shines in Italy’s Motor Valley, the credit belongs to those who worked — and still work — there. It occupies a place alongside Ferrari and Lamborghini, Dallara, Pagani and Maserati.

Growth was never linear. In the 1980s came Cagiva, owned by the Castiglioni brothers. In 1993, the Monster, designed by Miguel Galluzzi, became one of the models that symbolised Ducati’s rebirth. Three years later, in 1996, the American fund Texas Pacific Group came in, bringing fresh capital and a more international approach to management.

The company survived a serious financial crisis. In 2006, control passed to Investindustrial, and in 2007 Casey Stoner won Ducati’s first MotoGP world championship.

The bike has captivated many riders, including Valentino Rossi, who spent two years with Ducati without making his mark. Then came Andrea Dovizioso and Jorge Lorenzo. And then Pecco Bagnaia, with his two world titles in eight years. Today it is Marc Márquez, seeking to repeat his 2025 championship triumph.

So many riders have climbed aboard the Red of Borgo Panigale — each compelling in his own way.

The decisive change came in 2012, when Volkswagen, through Audi, bought Ducati for €747 million. The previous year, the company had sold 42,016 motorcycles and generated revenue of €479 million.

Today its heart remains in Borgo Panigale, but Ducati is a multinational company operating at the most prestigious end of the motorcycle market. Yet finance and figures still do not tell the whole story. Ducati rallies are born of devotion.

The company is present in more than 90 countries, with around 800 dealerships and service centres. In 2025, it delivered 50,895 motorcycles, generated revenue of €925 million and posted an operating profit of €52 million.

This September, as Volkswagen confirmed that it was also reviewing its stake in Ducati, analysts cited by Bloomberg put the value of the entire company at around €1.25 billion.

But it is clear that the figure represents more than motorcycles and factories. It includes the brand, the technology, the global network and the racing heritage.

items.title: The rebirth of the Golden Room: inside Milan’s Poldi Pezzoli house museum
items.summary: Following a restoration funded by the World Monuments Fund, the residence’s most iconic room has finally reopened to the public. The space—which houses Renaissance masterpieces, historic clocks, and precious Murano glass—now reveals a magnificent window that had been hidden from view for 50 years
items.content:
MILAN — Two hundred lire for every week of delay. That was the fine stipulated in the contract if the grand reception room of a house just steps from Milan’s Duomo and La Scala opera house was not completed by September 15, 1876.

Gian Giacomo Poldi Pezzoli , a Milanese nobleman and passionate art collector, had assembled some of the finest sculptors, cabinetmakers and fresco painters from the Brera Academy of Fine Arts, one of the world’s most prestigious art institutions. He had entrusted the project to Giuseppe Bertini.

The contracts, signed in March of that year, reveal the full extent of the splendour Poldi Pezzoli envisioned. The room was intended to house the most precious pieces in his collection, including Renaissance masterpieces, and its surroundings had to be worthy of the works on display.

The walls were to be decorated with frescoes and draped in damask fabric, while paintings would rest on pedestals to create a more intimate atmosphere. Above visitors’ heads would rise a gilded wooden coffered ceiling, from which the room would take its name.

Natural light would flood in through a large Palladian window overlooking the palazzo’s garden. Designed with columns topped by bronze capitals and rosettes decorating its central arch, the window was to be made from coloured marble. Samples of green marble from Varallo, purple-veined marble from Siena, and marble from Carrara and Candoglia were specially transported to Milan by rail.

Despite the contractual penalty, construction dragged on well beyond the agreed deadline. The house museum, with works by Pollaiolo, Mantegna, Botticelli, Raphael, Piero della Francesca, Tiepolo, Canaletto and Hayez, alongside extraordinary collections of clocks, Murano glass and Meissen porcelain, finally opened to the public in 1881. Poldi Pezzoli, who had died in 1879, never lived to see his vision completed.

Today, 150 years after the conception of this pioneering house museum, which went on to inspire institutions around the world, including the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and the Frick Collection in the United States, the Golden Room has reopened following an ambitious restoration that has transformed the museum’s most emblematic space.

The €250,000 project was funded by the World Monuments Fund, the international private non-profit organisation dedicated to preserving some of the world’s most valuable cultural heritage sites, which opened its Milan office this spring.

The false ceiling installed in the 1970s has been removed, restoring the room’s coffered ceiling. This time, however, it is ivory rather than the gilded version of the 19th century.

The imposing architecture of the window designed by sculptor Lodovico Pogliaghi, creator of the main bronze doors of Milan Cathedral, has also been brought back into view.

And there is more. The room has regained its warmth thanks to dark green walls that echo the marble of the Palladian window. The wooden mirror frame with Murano glass has been restored, while two 17th-century tapestries are once again on display, along with 40 of the 98 decorative ceiling panels from the postwar redesign, which had been lying in storage for years.

“The work began with a study of the archival documents,” explains Alessandra Quarto, director of the house museum and the driving force behind a programme to revitalise its historic interiors that began in 2023.

The archives yielded the original contracts, payment records and period photographs documenting the room’s many transformations.

“Last June, we carried out video inspections to establish what remained of the original structure above the false ceiling installed in the 1970s,” Quarto explains.

The inspections revealed that the wooden ceiling created after the war by Fernanda Wittgens, the art historian who saved numerous Milanese masterpieces from wartime bombing, had been completely demolished.

“But the marble arch of the window, complete with its bronze rosettes, was clearly still there and had survived in excellent condition,” the director adds.

Over the past 150 years, the Golden Room has undergone several transformations.

The first came after the bombing of 1943, which destroyed part of its 19th-century interior. Years of restoration work and debate over how the museum should be rebuilt followed, until it finally reopened in 1951 with an interior designed by Wittgens herself.

The destroyed fireplace was replaced with a similar one borrowed from Sforza Castle, while the coffered ceiling was reconstructed and decorated with 98 painted panels donated by the Italian state as compensation for the damage the museum had suffered.

In 1974, the room underwent another transformation. Reflecting the prevailing thinking of the time, a more restrained design was chosen to give greater prominence to the artworks on display.

The ceiling was therefore demolished and replaced with a plasterboard structure forming a shallow vault, one metre lower than the original ceiling.

The redesign came at the expense of part of the window, the decorative ceiling panels — half of which were installed in the galleries devoted to the Lombard Renaissance — and the tapestries depicting The Adventures of Amadis of Gaul by Françoise Spiering, which had adorned the room since the late 19th century.

Now, at last, the Golden Room has regained its original proportions. And its magnificent marble window, hidden from view for half a century.

items.title: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round of Brazil election
items.summary: With neither candidate getting more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.
items.content:
Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of an outright majority.

There will be a run-off between the two candidates on 25 October.

Bolsonaro is the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election.

Sunday's vote was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With almost all of the votes counted, Bolsonaro has 47% to Lula's 45% of the vote.

Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other candidates knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.

His Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.

The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America's largest country and economy – will follow suit.

After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".

Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".

Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters.

Lula is more popular in Brazil's poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.

He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil's history.

After that election, Bolsonaro's supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023.

Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro's wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday.

Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the 8 January riots, amnesty if elected.

He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.

Bolsonaro said on Sunday he was "very happy" to have led Lula in the first-round vote, and expressed confidence that he would clinch a run-off victory in three weeks' time.

"I am very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government," he said, according to AFP.

Lula said the outcome of the vote was "unexpected", but insisted the race was not over.

"I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round," he said on Sunday. "The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people."

The president of Brazil's supreme electoral court said on Sunday that no evidence of international interference was found in the election.

President Lula made "sovereignty" a key pillar of his campaign and at times accused the US of trying to interfere in and influence Brazil's elections - which the US has denied.

Earlier this year, Bolsonaro successfully lobbied the US to designate the two biggest Brazilian gangs as terrorist organisations.

Last year, Donald Trump used the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro as justification for imposing tariffs on Brazil and sanctioning some top officials and judges.

A win for Flávio Bolsonaro would likely see Brazil join the US's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking and align more closely with the US.

Corruption became a key issue in this campaign after a scandal involving a jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiling senior figures across the political spectrum.

Bolsonaro acknowledged that he'd asked Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).

Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to the Supreme Court judge Alexandre de Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing.

Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.

Crime and insecurity were also top concerns for voters. Brazil's homicide rate has fallen, but street crime such as phone thefts, that are highly visible to voters, have increased - and violence and drug trafficking are still major problems.

Bolsonaro has pledged to designate Brazilian gangs as terrorists and build maximum-security prisons akin to those in El Salvador. His father, during his presidency, loosened gun ownership restrictions.

Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons.

The economy has also been central to this campaign: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth.

Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, most notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty.

He has also backed oil drilling exploration , which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro's presidency.

Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.

items.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
items.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
items.content:
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.

Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.

Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.

Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.

The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.

Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.

"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.

More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.

"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).

If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.

On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".

But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.

That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.

To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.

"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.

It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.

Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.

"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.

Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.

China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.

Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.

A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.

On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.

"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."

The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.

But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.

India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.

"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."

More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.

"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.

"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

items.title: In Brasile ci sarà il ballottaggio tra Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula
items.summary: Al primo turno delle elezioni presidenziali nessuno dei due è andato oltre il 50 per cento, ma Bolsonaro è messo un po' meglio
items.content:
Al primo turno delle elezioni presidenziali in Brasile nessun candidato è andato oltre il 50 per cento dei voti, e per questo ci sarà un turno di ballottaggio tra i due più votati: il presidente uscente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , di sinistra, e il candidato di estrema destra Flávio Bolsonaro, figlio dell’ex presidente Jair, che sta scontando una condanna a 27 anni per aver tentato di organizzare un colpo di stato nel 2022. Il ballottaggio è previsto per domenica 25 ottobre.

Flávio Bolsonaro è quello che è andato più vicino alla soglia del 50 per cento: è al 47 per cento circa delle preferenze , mentre Lula è al 45. C’erano altri dieci candidati: nessuno di loro ha superato il 3 per cento e la maggior parte non è arrivata nemmeno all’1. L’affluenza è stata del 79 per cento, in linea con le precedenti elezioni presidenziali.

Un distacco di 2 punti non è incolmabile per Lula in vista del ballottaggio, ma Bolsonaro partirà necessariamente favorito, e questo potrebbe influenzare un po’ le prossime tre settimane di campagna elettorale: finora i due erano sempre stati molto vicini nei sondaggi, ma Flávio Bolsonaro era pur sempre un candidato senza esperienza politica e lo sfidante del presidente uscente. Anche alle ultime elezioni nel 2022 si andò al ballottaggio, quella volta tra Lula e Bolsonaro padre, Jair, ma al primo turno Lula aveva preso 5 punti in più.

Lula ha 80 anni ed è al suo terzo mandato da presidente. I primi due furono tra il 2003 e il 2011, e non si era potuto ricandidare perché in Brasile non si possono fare più di due mandati consecutivi. In campagna elettorale non aveva grandi risultati da mostrare: ha ottenuto buoni risultati nell’economia, ma con un rallentamento nell’ultimo anno e un problema significativo di debito pubblico. È stato criticato soprattutto per la gestione della criminalità e da destra accusato di clientelismo e assistenzialismo per le misure sociali che hanno aiutato le famiglie più povere, mentre è stata apprezzata la contrapposizione ai dazi e alle ingerenze degli Stati Uniti.

Anche per questo ha impostato la sua comunicazione soprattutto sulla contrapposizione con la famiglia Bolsonaro, che a queste elezioni era molto presente al di là del candidato Flávio, che di anni ne ha 45. Innanzitutto con Jair, che è agli arresti domiciliari ma compariva regolarmente in immagini e video durante i comizi del figlio, attraverso avatar creati con l’intelligenza artificiale o espedienti simili. Il figlio lo ha citato di continuo, anche sfruttando una notevole somiglianza fisica, ma ha anche cercato di proporsi come leggermente più moderato su alcune questioni.

C’erano poi altri membri della famiglia candidati in parlamento, e sono stati tutti eletti: alla Camera è stato eletto Renan Jair Bolsonaro, di 28 anni, al suo primo mandato. Al Senato è stato eletto Carlos, che in passato aveva già lavorato per il padre a capo di una struttura che si occupava di attaccare gli avversari politici sui social, anche con insulti e notizie false, rinominata «gabinetto dell’odio».

E sempre al Senato è stata eletta anche Michelle Bolsonaro, terza moglie di Jair, pastora evangelica e protagonista di un’enorme evoluzione politica, da timida moglie del candidato Jair nel 2018 a seguitissima e carismatica leader dell’ala femminile del Partito Liberale, quello dei Bolsonaro appunto.

Flávio ha promesso che in caso di vittoria darà la grazia al padre (nel caso, ci sarebbero conseguenze legali enormi e probabilmente una crisi costituzionale). Ci si aspetta poi che possa riabilitare il fratello Eduardo, che vive negli Stati Uniti e in Brasile è stato condannato a quattro anni e due mesi di carcere per aver provato a influenzare il processo al padre attraverso uno stato straniero (gli Stati Uniti): potrebbe così farlo tornare e magari dargli un incarico di rilievo nel governo.

items.title: L’emergenza casa investe tutta Europa. In Italia 3 milioni in crisi
items.summary: Nella Ue le difficoltà interessano il 7,7% della popolazione. Da Berlino a New York l’impegno dei nuovi sindaci
items.content:
ROMA – Migliaia di spagnoli in piazza con tintinnar di chiavi , per protestare contro la bocciatura di una legge sul diritto all’abitare presentata dal governo Sanchez. Una sindaca di estrema sinistra, Elif Eralp, eletta a Berlino con la promessa di socializzare 200 mila appartamenti di proprietà di grandi gruppi immobiliari. Un sindaco molto progressista, Zohran Mamdani, che a New York ha messo al primo punto del programma ha la costruzione di 200 mila nuove abitazioni a prezzi abbordabili e il blocco dei canoni di affitto. Nelle grandi metropoli del mondo, e in quelle d’Europa, il tema dell’accessibilità – o meglio: inaccessibilità – della casa torna al pettine del dibattito politico. Mobilita cittadini altrimenti abulici, orienta elezioni. Suggerisce a tutti i governi, al di là del colore, di mettere sul tavolo più o meno credibili Piani casa. E offre a una sinistra alla disperata ricerca di temi identitari e popolari un terreno su cui recuperare voti.

È il terreno di una crisi abitativa, di cui i numeri restituiscono solo in parte le proporzioni storiche ed emotive. Ha una parte di emergenza acuta, il 7,7% di cittadini europei e il 5% degli italiani, circa 3 milioni di persone, che vivono in condizioni di stress abitativo, per cui la rata del mutuo o il costo dell’affitto mangia oltre il 40% del reddito disponibile. Ma non si ferma più lì. Perché dal Covid in poi, una fiammata di inflazione dopo l’altra, acquisti e affitti sono diventati inaccessibili per una fascia crescente della popolazione, ceto medio impoverito, giovani al primo impiego, studenti senza fortune familiari, nuclei monoreddito . Specie nelle grandi città-calamita, quelle dove gli aspiranti residenti devono competere per ogni metro quadro con fondi immobiliari, investitori privati e affitti turistici.

Ogni città ha le sue peculiarità. Ma quasi ovunque una politica nazionale disinteressata e amministrazioni locali deboli hanno consentito per anni che il mercato seguisse la legge del massimo profitto, che non va d’accordo con accessibilità e inclusione. Dal 2013 i prezzi medi al metro quadro in Europa sono saliti del 60%, e molto più nelle aree urbane. Anche dove i salari sono aumentati non hanno tenuto il passo. Meno del 7% dello stock abitativo europeo è edilizia pubblica e tra il 2018 e il 2024 - dice la Commissione - gli Airbnb sono raddoppiati. Nel frattempo il 20% delle case è vuoto, perché in aree interne dove nessuno vuole vivere o perché di proprietà di chi non ha bisogno di affittarle.

E l’Italia? Bel paradosso . Siamo il Paese dei proprietari di case, oltre l’80% delle famiglie, cosa che limita - per lo più a residenti stranieri, senza grande rappresentanza - le sacche di disagio abitativo acuto. Siamo anche l’unico Paese dove i prezzi restano sotto il picco toccato prima della grande crisi del 2008. D’altra parte i salari sono fermi da trent’anni, e questo rende comunque l’acquisto sempre meno accessibile. Così cresce la pressione sul mercato dell’affitto, dove l’offerta è scarsissima e i prezzi in costante rialzo. «Questo sta rendendo alcuni territori e aree metropolitane i navvicinabili per un crescente numero di persone», scrive Nomisma nel suo Osservatorio. Milano, ovvio, ma anche Bologna, Roma, Verona, Napoli.

I tentativi di risposta a livello globale vanno in due direzioni diverse, anche se non per forza inconciliabili. La prima è tornare a costruire case dove la domanda è alta: edilizia pubblica oppure, per chi non ha i soldi o la vocazione, in convenzione con i privati, come nel Piano casa del governo Meloni. La seconda è regolare in maniera più stringente il mercato, i canoni, le locazioni turistiche, il ruolo dei fondi: limitare il mattone-investimento per preservare il mattone-residenza, con il rischio, in Italia ben noto, di scontentare il popolo di Boomer che su prima, seconda o terza casa ci ha investito per anni i risparmi. È il modello del decreto di Sanchez in Spagna. Nel suo piano per l’abitare sostenibile la Commissione le prova entrambe, più case e più regole, ma con pochi fondi e grande timidezza.

items.title: Forced to call him 'Dad': Trial over sexual abuse in disabled care home shocks South Korea
items.summary: The BBC spoke to one of three residents at a care home who were sexually assaulted by a staff member.
items.content:
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.

She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.

Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.

The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.

The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.

We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.

Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.

The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.

According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.

Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.

That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.

She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.

Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.

According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.

As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.

"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.

When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."

A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.

They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.

Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.

He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.

For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".

A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.

The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.

In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.

The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.

But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.

According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.

Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.

Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".

But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.

"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.

Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".

Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.

Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".

Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."

The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".

The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.

That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.

These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.

But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.

A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.

The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.

Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.

Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.

One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.

Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.

And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.

In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.

In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.

"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."

The stop motion work of Phil Tippett and the now closed Tippett Studios is being preserved in a free-to-browse online archive.

August brought with it the sad news that Tippett Studios, the Berkeley-based animation and effects house founded by Phil Tippett, was closing down . The company had been in financial trouble for a while, and as it closed its doors on the 28th of that month, decades of props, memorabilia and art was sold off in a two-day auction.

As if the closure itself – and Phil Tippett’s retirement – wasn’t sad enough news on its own, there was the fear that huge amounts of art stored in the studio was about to vanish into private collections, never to be seen again. Tippett was, after all, the animator whose work illuminated the likes of Star Wars, RoboCop, Starship Troopers and too many other classic movies to list.

There’s now happier news to report, though. An anonymous person was at the auction in August, spotted a folder of CD-ROMs and other discs, and managed to acquire it for an undisclosed sum. Rather than keep the contents of those discs to themselves, that person has now uploaded it all to the Internet Archive .

“I quickly realized that some of this information wasn’t available online and might not ever be in the future in such high resolution,” the donor, who simply calls themselves ‘TippettFan’, writes. “So I purchased the disc folder and digitized all of its contents. What you have here are .ISO image files of the 90 key, non-duplicated discs from Tippett’s archives.”

There are a few clips in there that are available to view online, including test clips of CGI creatures and an interview with Phil Tippett from 2008. The bulk of the archive, however, is all in the .ISO disc image format the donor mentioned above – and there are gigabytes of files to download and comb through ( listed here ), with filenames describing behind the scenes images from RoboCop and Starship Troopers , slides of Tippett’s work on the original Star Wars, and, unexpectedly, publicity stills from the calamitous Catwoman .

In short, there’s a ton of film history here, and it’ll likely take weeks for historians and fans to comb through. We’ll be going through some of it ourselves, undoubtedly, and will report back if we find anything we think you might find interesting.

For now, though, what a treasure trove. Thank you to TippettFan, whoever you are, and thanks too to Brandon Sheffield for highlighting the archive on BlueSky.

items.title: Turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and get its disk space back
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49957116 Points: 700 # Comments: 465
items.content:
Turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and remove its downloaded models.

macOS 27 no longer has a single switch for Apple Intelligence, and its models stay on disk after the features are turned off. RemoveMacAI turns the features off, removes the models and prevents macOS from downloading them again. All changes can be reverted.

The script downloads the latest release, verifies its SHA-256 checksum and runs it from a temporary directory. Nothing is installed.

Every release is built from its tag by GitHub Actions and carries a build provenance attestation. To check that a download came from this repository's source:

RemoveMacAI shows the current state and asks for confirmation. It then opens System Settings to install its configuration profile, which macOS requires the user to approve, and removes the models.

Model sizes that the asset service cannot report are shown as unknown . If model removal fails or cannot be confirmed, off exits with status 1 and leaves the configuration profile active. Check the reported warnings and run removemacai status before trying again.

Features turned off: Siri (including "Hey Siri" and the menu bar icon), Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, summaries in Mail, Messages, Safari, Notes and notifications, Mail smart replies, inline text predictions, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up and Xcode predictive code completion.

Models removed: the Apple Intelligence foundation models and the models for image generation and Genmoji, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up and Xcode code completion.

Does dictation still work? Yes. Dictation is a separate setting, and its speech models are not removed.

Do macOS updates undo the changes? No. The profile, including the download block, persists across updates.

Storage settings still lists Apple Intelligence after the models were deleted. Apple's asset service releases the models right away, but macOS deletes the files on its own schedule. Until then, System Settings > General > Storage keeps counting them under Apple Intelligence.

Why is a process named Siri still running? In macOS 27 the Spotlight window runs as a process named Siri. Some system services also stay loaded; they are protected by System Integrity Protection.

What stops working? The features listed above, apps that use Apple's on-device models (the Foundation Models framework and the Use Model action in Shortcuts), Visual Intelligence and natural-language editing in Calendar.

Run removemacai revert , then brew uninstall removemacai if it was installed with Homebrew.

RemoveMacAI is built on pared , a complete working tool by 4evy that first mapped the asset service, the model sets and several of the settings keys. Its license is in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md .

items.title: Mosquitoes Are a Choice
items.summary: Article URL: https://worksinprogress.co/issue/mosquitoes-are-a-choice/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49956290 Points: 63 # Comments: 52
items.content:
Most Americans think of mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, yellow fever, and dengue as problems that affect people in other countries, not their own. Until recently, they would have been largely correct: malaria and yellow fever were eliminated in the United States in the twentieth century, and dengue had become extremely rare, with most cases brought back from abroad. But as temperatures have risen and mosquitoes have developed resistance to pesticides, these diseases have become a growing problem again in the United States.

In 2024, the country reported almost 4,000 cases of dengue, a 360 percent increase over the average of 830 per year over the previous decade; Florida, California, and Texas all saw locally acquired transmission; and Puerto Rico declared dengue a public health emergency. Ten locally acquired malaria cases were reported nationwide in 2023, the first reported in twenty years. And though yellow fever remains gone for now, the mosquitoes capable of spreading it are still present.

But we don’t have to accept this threat. We have new ways to wipe out mosquito-borne diseases with minimal environmental cost. The United States is sufficiently well-resourced, and its disease-carrying mosquito population sufficiently small, that it can stamp out this problem entirely within its own borders.

The reason we haven’t is that the technology has spent fifteen years in regulatory limbo. Ending this impasse would allow us to eliminate many mosquito-borne diseases from the United States, and eventually the rest of the world.

Genetic engineering can suppress mosquitoes: researchers insert a gene into male mosquitoes that means their offspring will not survive, and then release them into the wild, where they mate with females, prevent those females having any surviving offspring, and collapse local populations. In 2000 , biologists at the University of Oxford demonstrated that this idea could work in fruit flies. They engineered the flies to carry a gene that makes a protein called tTAV, harmless in small amounts but lethal when it builds up. In the lab, the insects are reared in a medium laced with the antibiotic tetracycline, which keeps the gene switched off. But, in the wild, where there is no tetracycline, the gene switches on, and the offspring die before adulthood.

The scientists then formed a company, Oxitec, which was intended to work with governments to research and deploy the technology. They engineered the same gene into male Aedes aegypti , the mosquito that spreads dengue and yellow fever. In this strain, the lethal effect is tuned to kill only the female offspring, while the males survive and pass the gene on for a few generations before it disappears. This approach means the gene continues driving down mosquito numbers for several generations without needing a fresh ‘top up’ of engineered males, but it is also self-limiting: the females that inherit it die off each generation, so the lethal gene steadily declines in the wild. Yet the technique is hugely effective. Sustained releases cut a wild Aedes aegypti population in the Cayman Islands by 80 percent , and in a field trial in Juazeiro, Brazil by about 95 percent . The company submitted its data to seek approval in the United States in 2010. But it has been slow going.

Until that point, engineered insects had been used only for agricultural pest control. Since the 1950s, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA ) had been using the ‘sterile insect technique’, sterilizing male insects with radiation rather than genetic modification, which would mate with wild females and produce no offspring, steadily driving the wild population down. The technique’s major success was in fighting screwworm: an extremely nasty insect that lays its eggs in open wounds, and whose larvae then hatch and burrow into the flesh of any animal unlucky enough to be afflicted (usually livestock), killing them within days. The United States used the sterile insect technique to clear out this pest in the 1960s, and eventually pushed it back as far as the southern tip of Panama. This is estimated to have saved American cattle farmers close to $800 million per year , with billions more in benefits to the wider economy. But containment broke, and in June 2026 , Texas detected the United States’ first case of screwworm in 60 years, likely aided by cattle smuggling from Central America, where the pest has resurged. With billions of dollars in damages, Texas officials are once again deploying sterile flies to contain its spread.

The Mediterranean fruit fly, which attacks more than 300 kinds of fruit and vegetables and is considered the most destructive fruit pest in the world, has been beaten back the same way, with sterile flies released over California and Florida. It’s estimated that, if the fruit fly resettles in California, the resulting crop damage could cost over a billion dollars per year in that state alone.

When Oxitec first sought approval for its gene-edited Aedes , it applied to the agency that had long managed mass insect releases, the USDA . But it took a year and a half for the USDA to reject the application and inform the company that it should instead apply to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The FDA had claimed jurisdiction over genetically modified animals under its authority over veterinary drugs. Its guidance stated that ‘altered genomic DNA in an animal is a drug … because such altered DNA is an article intended to affect the structure or function of the body of the animal’. Until then, the USDA’s insects had been sterilized through radiation, which damages an insect’s sperm so that it leaves no viable offspring. Oxitec, by contrast, had inserted a new gene. Even so, the category was a poor fit for Oxitec’s mosquitoes.

Oxitec’s application sat with the FDA for another five years. Like the USDA, the FDA could not work out how to apply existing rules for veterinary drugs to an engineered mosquito, eventually concluding that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which oversees pesticide registration, was a better fit. The FDA issued new guidance stating that they did not regulate products ‘intended to prevent, destroy, repel, or mitigate mosquitoes for population control purposes.’ The FDA had essentially created a bespoke carve-out for genetically engineered mosquitoes, recognizing that its regulatory frameworks weren’t set up to evaluate something like this.

In its third review, at the EPA, Oxitec’s mosquitoes were subject to the rules governing pesticides, which often require both scientific assessments and field trials before the product can be lawfully sold and distributed. In May 2020 , a full decade after Oxitec first sought approval, the EPA granted them an Experimental Use Permit, which didn’t allow them to sell their product but did finally allow them to test it to obtain the safety and efficacy data needed for commercial registration by running field trials in delimited areas.

The location they chose for those field trials was the Florida Keys, an island chain off the southern tip of Florida, where dengue had resurged . Local authorities were eager to use genetically modified mosquitoes and in 2021 , Oxitec ran the first field trials in the United States that demonstrated female mosquitoes that inherited the gene died before adulthood. In 2022, the EPA expanded the trials to California, clearing the release of up to 2.4 billion genetically engineered mosquitoes across the two states, but the releases were paused after public pushback.

Oxitec’s permit expired in April 2024, meaning no further mosquitoes could be released without new authorization from the EPA. A full commercial registration requires another review from the agency, this one focused on field trial data. Their full registration remains pending , over two years after the end of their field trial permit. A scientific advisory panel reviewing the case was supposed to convene in November 2025 , but the meeting was postponed with, at the time of writing, no new date set. As Florida Keys Mosquito Control District Executive Director Andrea Leal said, ‘our biggest challenges have been awaiting regulatory approvals.’ Luckily, this district had another mosquito control option to try out: Wolbachia -infected mosquitoes.

Around the same time as genetically engineered mosquitoes were becoming viable, an alternative technique emerged. It rests on a bacterium called Wolbachia, which naturally infects roughly 60 percent of insect species, including butterflies, fruit flies, and bees. Wolbachia has two effects on insects that make it useful for preventing mosquito-borne disease. First, it makes them less able to carry viruses, including those that infect humans. Second, the bacterium is passed on to future generations – specifically, infected females pass it on through their eggs, and infected males can only produce offspring if they mate with infected females; if they mate with uninfected females, the offspring will not develop. By releasing infected male and female mosquitoes, wild mosquito populations can be seeded with Wolbachia until most of them carry it, becoming resistant to viruses like dengue and spreading their resistance to future generations. And since this approach does not involve genetic modification, it ought to be able to bypass much of the regulation that stalled Oxitec’s gene-modified Aedes .
